sections.html:
• Other names: Topshell snail, Trochus shell, Star snail, Conehead snail
  • Scientific name: Lithopoma tectum (synonyms: Astraea tecta, Trochus tectus)
  • Minimum tank: 5 gallons (about 20 litres)
  • Keeping: easy; breeding: medium
  • Size (shell): up to 6 cm
  • Specific gravity: 1.021–1.026
  • Optimal KH: 7–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: herbivorous
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colour: reddish-orange to creamy-white

The Astrea snail is not a rare saltwater snail; it can be bought almost everywhere. It is a good addition to the tank in terms of looks and also helps keep the tank clean of waste and algae. However, sometimes they also need some cleaning.

Astrea snails can have their own pests in the form of tiny pyramid snails. These parasites can even kill their host, so check your snails and remove any pyramid snails as soon as possible.

The scientific name 'Astraea tecta' is routinely used in the trade, but it is wrong: it is not included in the WoRMS database. Biologists use the synonyms 'Trochus tectus', now known as 'Lithopoma tectum'. Misidentification in the trade is a fundamental issue. There are look-alike species, such as the Fenestrate Top Snail (Tectus fenestratus), which are not as hardy as the Astrea snail and may require a different setup with colder water. People may therefore think the species is not good enough for their aquarium when in reality it is not even an Astrea snail.
Typical colonies of the Astrea snail occur in the shallows of the Caribbean Sea, the Gulf of Mexico and the Lesser Antilles, and in the Atlantic Ocean off Brazil.

Astrea snails live on outer reef flats and reef crests with abundant stony corals, on areas of turf algae for adults, and on intertidal reef flats with stony coral or rubble bottom for juveniles. They prefer higher-energy environments where they can graze tough macroalgae and crustose coralline algae growing on hard substrates.

The optimum depth for these snails is between 1 m and 10 m, although they can be found as deep as 15 m.
These snails can live in the smallest marine tank. Depending on your livestock, a small tank (5 gallons, or 20 litres) can be good enough for a few Astrea snails.

True Astrea snails can survive, grow and function even in sub-optimal water conditions. Their hardy nature makes them easy to care for, so both veterans and beginners can keep this species.

Nonetheless, as with any aquarium inhabitant, make sure the tank is set up correctly and the water is properly cycled, so that the right bacteria convert harmful compounds into less harmful ones.

Astrea snails do not need lighting; they are most active at night. Lighting should be adapted to the needs of fish, corals, sea anemones and so on.

Although Astrea snails are extremely adaptable to a wide range of water parameters, they still have some preferences. They thrive in warm water. The temperature should stay in the range of about 22 to 27°C, with 22–24°C optimal. It is advisable to install a heater and thermometer to keep the water constant.

The pH should be kept around 8.1 to 8.4 and alkalinity in the range of 7 to 12 dKH, although these often go a little higher or lower. Specific gravity should be between 1.021 and 1.026. Nitrate should be below 20 ppm.

Most care guides say Astrea snails are sensitive to even small changes in water values. According to an experiment, however, Astrea snails survived without any losses when salinity was reduced by almost 50%. Low salinity was maintained in the treatment buckets for an additional 20 minutes, followed by a rapid increase back to ambient levels. That kind of stress increased their hunger and they consumed more algae than non-stressed snails.

Home experiments of this type are not encouraged, and careful acclimation is still recommended, as with all invertebrates. Do it very slowly; in general, 2–3 hours is good enough.

Basic tank equipment: filter (Marineland Penguin Power), aquarium pump (Tetra Whisper air pump), heater (Tetra HT Submersible), substrate (Nature's Ocean), live rock (Carib Sea), sea salt (Instant Ocean marine salt), test kit (API Aquarium Water Test Kit) and a salinity refractometer or hydrometer.

Astrea snails are herbivorous and great scavengers. They graze on corals and rocks for microscopic algae, cyanobacteria and diatoms. They use a strong, rasping radula to scrape hair algae, brown algae, green algae and filamentous algae from rocks and boulders in the tank.

The only snails that outperform them are turbo snails. However, the small size of Astrea snails allows them to reach holes and crevices that other members of the clean-up crew cannot.

In the aquarium they also feed on leftover shrimp or fish food such as pills, flakes, pellets, algae/spirulina wafers and frozen foods.

Astrea snails need a lot of food, so be prepared to supplement with herbivore pellets (algae pellets, dried algae and so on) if there is not enough algae growth.

Astrea snails are sensitive to copper and copper compounds.

Like all snails, Astrea snails need calcium, either in the diet or in the water (ideally both), to keep their shells hard enough. Keeping calcium levels between 350 and 450 ppm is best.

Astrea snails are non-aggressive, solitary and docile by nature, liking a calm environment and peaceful tank mates. They have no means to attack other tank inhabitants and only their operculum and shell to protect them from aggressors.

Astrea snails are nocturnal. Their activity peaks at dusk and gradually stops during the night, before sunrise. Smaller snails are more active, with more intense and longer movements. This nocturnal behaviour is not uncommon for grazing gastropods and is mainly associated with avoiding visual predators while feeding.

Astrea snails are not shy and do not scare easily. When placed on the bottom of the tank, they soon crawl onto the corals and explore all the crevices.

As they reach adult size, their climbing ability gets worse, so do not expect them to clean the side glass. Keep in mind that an Astrea snail has difficulty righting itself if it falls or is knocked upside down, so it is advisable to check from time to time whether any have ended up upside down.

They are not burrowers and spend the vast majority of their time below the waterline, so the risk of escaping is quite low.

They are reef safe: they will not damage anything in a reef tank and will not try to eat corals. Their small size also prevents them from knocking over freestanding corals on the bottom.
Astrea snails are gonochoric (separate male and female individuals), without any external sexual dimorphism.

According to observations, they reach reproductive maturity at 6–8 months old. Astrea snails are broadcast spawners and fertilisation takes place in the water column.

Spawning is initiated by males, and females spawn in response to sperm in the water. Females generally spawn for 5–10 minutes, releasing more than 1 million oocytes (unfertilised eggs). The eggs are covered in transparent mucus and float in the seawater. The water will clear soon enough; in a community tank, corals and other filter feeders eat the particles that make the water cloudy.

Spawning often occurs in synchrony with lunar or tidal cycles, generally at night and within one or two nights of a full or new moon. In nature, spawning occurs throughout the year in low latitudes and only during the warmer months in higher latitudes.

The developmental period is comparatively short, and hatching occurs about 12–24 hours after fertilisation, when the larvae reach the planktonic phase. The larvae then emerge as free-swimming veligers. This stage lasts approximately 3–5 days, after which the veligers settle onto the reef substrate and begin grazing on fine filamentous algae and microorganisms. In the ocean, settlement may be delayed by about 10 days when suitable substrate is unavailable. The larvae begin to gradually metamorphose to the crawling stage at 6 to 8 days.

Although females can release more than 1 million eggs, the mortality rate is very high and only a few survive to become adults. Unlike adults, Astrea snail larvae cannot survive low salinity. Fertilisation, larval development and larval metamorphosis are suppressed at salinities lower than 30‰.

Most snails are peaceful and solitary, and Astrea snails are no exception. They are good companions for dwarf shrimp and small non-carnivorous fish. They are compatible with, for example:

  • shrimp such as Sexy Shrimp, Red Fire shrimp (Lysmata debelius), Peppermint shrimp (Lysmata wurdemanni) or Skunk Cleaner (Lysmata amboinensis)
  • snails such as Bumble Bee Snail, Fighting Conch Snail, Cerith snails, Mexican turbo snails, Trochus snails and others

An adult Bumble Bee Snail can attack small Astrea snails if there is not enough food in the tank.

Under no circumstances keep Astrea snails with the orange claw hermit crab (Calcinus tibicen). In nature, 63.33% of these crabs preferentially occupy shells of Astraea tecta, and hermit crabs can try to kill the snails just for their shells. Be very careful with other hermit crabs too (such as the Halloween hermit crab and the blue leg hermit crab); ideally, do not keep hermit crabs and Astrea snails together. Upside-down snails are easy food for hermit crabs.

Coral banded shrimp (Stenopus hispidus) and crabs can also be dangerous for these snails.
